datasets.title: Datasets and the splits that keep you honest
datasets.description: Where training data comes from, what gets thrown away, and why one slice must never be trained on.

steps.heading: A pretraining mixture
steps.caption: Collection — raw sources arrive at wildly different scales and quality levels.

steps.heading: What survives filtering, per 100 raw web documents
steps.caption: Filtering — most of the crawl is discarded. Quality heuristics, language detection and safety filters cut it hard.

steps.heading: Three disjoint slices
steps.caption: Splitting — the surviving data is divided. Validation guides your decisions; test is touched once, at the end.

steps.heading: Reported accuracy with and without contamination
steps.caption: Leakage — if a test example also sits in training, the model recalls it instead of generalising and your metric becomes fiction.

steps.heading: Questions with no technical answer
steps.caption: Governance — licence, consent, PII and bias are properties of the dataset, so they become properties of the model.

preprocessing.title: Preprocessing: raw text to training records
preprocessing.description: The concrete transformations applied to one document before it can be used as a training example.

steps.heading: One crawled page
steps.caption: Raw scrape — HTML, navigation chrome and encoding noise surround the actual content.

steps.heading: Line-by-line decisions
steps.caption: Cleaning — markup is stripped, entities decoded, and boilerplate removed so only content text remains.

steps.heading: PII redaction
steps.caption: Privacy filtering — pattern matching and classifiers remove personal data before it can be memorised.

steps.heading: Copies of the same paragraph across the corpus
steps.caption: Deduplication — near-identical copies are collapsed. Duplicates make the model over-weight whatever happens to be repeated.

steps.heading: Filling a 2,048-token training sequence
steps.caption: Packing — cleaned documents are tokenised and concatenated to fill the sequence length exactly, so no compute is spent on padding.

tokenization-training.title: Training a tokenizer (BPE merges)
tokenization-training.description: Where the vocabulary comes from: counting adjacent pairs and merging the most frequent one, over and over.

steps.heading: Corpus sample "lower lowest slower" at merge 0
steps.caption: Start from bytes — before any merges, the vocabulary is just the 256 byte values. Every word is spelled out one character at a time.

steps.heading: Adjacent pair frequencies in the training corpus
steps.caption: Count pairs — every adjacent pair in the corpus is tallied. The most frequent pair wins the next merge slot.

steps.heading: After merge 1
steps.caption: Merge — "l"+"o" becomes the single token "lo" and is added to the vocabulary. The corpus is re-encoded and the count repeats.

steps.heading: The finished tokenizer on new text
steps.caption: After 30,000 merges — frequent words are one token, rare words are still assembled from pieces. Nothing is ever out-of-vocabulary.

steps.heading: Tokens needed for the same sentence, English-fitted vocabulary
steps.caption: Domain fit — a vocabulary fitted on English web text over-fragments code and other languages, making them slower and more expensive.

loss-function.title: Cross-entropy loss
loss-function.description: The number training actually minimises, and how it responds to the probability placed on the correct token.

steps.heading: p(next token | "The cat sat on the") before this update
steps.caption: The prediction — the model outputs a distribution over the vocabulary. The training text says the next token is " mat".

steps.heading: How the loss responds to p(correct)
steps.caption: Score it — cross-entropy looks only at the probability on the correct token: L = −log(0.499) = 0.7 nats.

steps.heading: Same prompt, after the update (hatched = before)
steps.caption: After a gradient step — the probability on " mat" rose, so the loss fell from 0.7 to 0.09 nats.

steps.heading: Pretraining loss over a run
steps.caption: Averaged over everything — the reported training loss is this quantity averaged across every token in every batch.

steps.heading: What low loss does and does not buy
steps.caption: Loss is a proxy, not a goal — it measures likelihood of the observed text. It says nothing about truth, safety or usefulness.

gradient-descent.title: Gradient descent: taking the step
gradient-descent.description: Given gradients, how parameters actually move — and what the learning rate does to that movement. (Computing the gradients is backpropagation, the next concept.)

steps.heading: Current state
steps.caption: Where we are — the parameter sits at w = −2. The gradient at that point is ∇L = 2(w−3) = −10: the slope points steeply downhill to the right.

steps.heading: Before and after one update with η = 0.3
steps.caption: The step — move against the gradient, scaled by the learning rate: w ← w − 0.3 × (−10) = 1.0. One step, a big improvement.

steps.heading: Loss over six updates, η = 0.3
steps.caption: Repeat — six steps at η = 0.3 land the parameter essentially on the optimum, with the loss flattening out at its minimum of 1.

steps.heading: Same loss surface, three learning rates
steps.caption: Learning rate is the whole game — too small crawls, too large overshoots so badly that the loss grows every step.

steps.heading: Full-batch versus mini-batch descent
steps.caption: Stochastic in practice — the true gradient over the full dataset is unaffordable, so each step uses a noisy estimate from one mini-batch.

backpropagation.title: Backpropagation: computing the gradients
backpropagation.description: Before anything can be updated, every parameter needs to know how much it contributed to the loss. That is a backward pass, not an update.

steps.heading: Forward: compute activations and the loss
steps.caption: Forward pass — inputs flow through the layers and produce a prediction. Every intermediate activation is stored, because the backward pass will need it.

steps.heading: Backward step 1: gradient at the output
steps.caption: Start at the loss — the first derivative is ∂L/∂a₃, how much the loss changes if the output changes. Everything else is derived from this.

steps.heading: The product being accumulated, layer by layer
steps.caption: Chain rule backwards — each layer multiplies the incoming gradient by its own local derivative and passes the result to the layer below.

steps.heading: Backward complete: ∂L/∂w for every weight
steps.caption: Every parameter gets a number — the gradient tells each weight the direction and size of its contribution to the loss. Nothing has moved yet.

steps.heading: One training step, split by responsibility
steps.caption: Hand-off — backpropagation stops here. The optimizer takes these gradients and decides the actual parameter update.

optimizers.title: Optimizers: turning gradients into updates
optimizers.description: Same gradients, same loss surface — three different rules for deciding how far and in which direction to actually move.

steps.heading: SGD, η = 0.15
steps.caption: Plain SGD — step directly against the gradient, every time. Simple, and it has no memory of the previous steps.

steps.heading: Momentum β = 0.9 versus plain SGD
steps.caption: Momentum — the update carries a velocity from previous steps, so consistent directions accelerate and noisy ones cancel out.

steps.heading: All three on the same problem
steps.caption: Adam — per-parameter adaptive step sizes from running mean and variance of the gradient. Rare parameters get larger effective steps.

steps.heading: GPU memory for a 7B model in mixed precision
steps.caption: The memory cost — Adam stores two extra numbers per parameter, so optimizer state can be twice the size of the model itself.

steps.heading: Effect of decoupled weight decay on parameter magnitude
steps.caption: Weight decay — AdamW additionally shrinks every weight slightly each step, discouraging large parameters and improving generalisation.

epochs-batches-lr.title: Epochs, batches and the learning-rate schedule
epochs-batches-lr.description: The rhythm of a training run: how data is grouped and how the step size changes over time.

steps.heading: 1,000,000 examples, batch size 256
steps.caption: Batch — a group of examples processed together to produce one gradient and one parameter update. Not one example, not the whole dataset.

steps.heading: Loss trajectory by batch size
steps.caption: Batch size trades noise against throughput — small batches give noisy gradients, large batches give smooth ones but need a matching learning rate.

steps.heading: Learning rate schedule (×10⁻⁴)
steps.caption: Warmup — the learning rate starts near zero and ramps up. Early full-size steps on a random initialisation frequently blow the run up.

steps.heading: Step size at three points in the run
steps.caption: Decay — the rate is annealed toward zero so late updates make small refinements instead of jumping out of the basin.

steps.heading: Which unit to quote
steps.caption: For LLMs, count tokens — pretraining usually makes a single pass or less over the corpus, so "epochs" stops being the useful unit.

pretraining-vs-finetuning.title: Pretraining vs fine-tuning
pretraining-vs-finetuning.description: Two stages that differ by three orders of magnitude in cost — and one risk that only appears in the second.

steps.heading: Scale comparison, log-ish
steps.caption: Pretraining — broad data, enormous scale, no particular task. The output is general capability with no manners.

steps.heading: Adapting a base model to clinical note summarisation
steps.caption: Fine-tuning — the same objective on narrow data. The weights start from the base rather than from random initialisation.

steps.heading: Two metrics during the same fine-tune
steps.caption: Catastrophic forgetting — push too hard on narrow data and the model gets better at your task while quietly losing general ability.

steps.heading: What each approach can and cannot fix
steps.caption: Cheaper alternatives first — most "we need to fine-tune" problems are actually prompt or retrieval problems.

steps.heading: What actually changes
steps.caption: Parameter-efficient methods — training a small adapter instead of all weights keeps the base intact and largely sidesteps forgetting.

sft.title: Supervised fine-tuning
sft.description: Teaching a completion engine to behave like an assistant, using demonstrations — and only scoring the part it should learn.

steps.heading: Base model, same prompt
steps.caption: The starting point — a base model continues text rather than answering it, because that is exactly what pretraining rewarded.

steps.heading: One training example
steps.caption: Demonstration data — curated pairs showing exactly the behaviour you want, in the chat format the model will see in production.

steps.heading: Which positions contribute to the loss
steps.caption: Loss masking — cross-entropy is applied only to the response tokens. The prompt is context, not something to be predicted.

steps.heading: Human preference win-rate versus dataset size
steps.caption: Quality over quantity — a few thousand carefully reviewed demonstrations beat hundreds of thousands of scraped ones.

steps.heading: After SFT
steps.caption: What SFT does not fix — it teaches the shape of a good answer, not truthfulness, and offers no way to express "this is better than that".

lora-qlora.title: LoRA and QLoRA
lora-qlora.description: Freeze the base, train a low-rank correction next to it, and watch the trainable parameter count collapse.

steps.heading: Full fine-tune of a 7B model in mixed precision
steps.caption: The problem — a full fine-tune updates every weight, so you need memory for the weights, their gradients and the optimizer state.

steps.heading: One attention projection matrix, d = 4,096
steps.caption: Freeze the base — W stops receiving updates. It still participates in the forward pass; it just never changes.

steps.heading: Trainable parameters for this one matrix
steps.caption: Inject a low-rank pair — A is 8×4096 and B is 4096×8. Their product has the same shape as W but only 65,536 parameters.

steps.heading: One adapted layer
steps.caption: Forward pass — the base output and the adapter output are added: h = Wx + B·A·x. At initialisation B = 0, so the model starts identical to the base.

steps.heading: Peak memory for the same 7B fine-tune
steps.caption: QLoRA — additionally store the frozen base in 4-bit. Memory drops far enough that a 7B fine-tune fits on one consumer GPU.

rlhf.title: RLHF: reward model plus policy optimisation
rlhf.description: Three separate models and a training loop. Compare this carefully with DPO, which removes most of it.

steps.heading: One labelled comparison
steps.caption: Collect preferences — humans compare two model answers and pick one. They rank; they do not write the ideal answer.

steps.heading: Reward model outputs after training
steps.caption: Train a reward model — a separate network learns to output a scalar score that ranks chosen above rejected on the collected pairs.

steps.heading: One PPO iteration
steps.caption: The RL loop — the policy samples an answer, the reward model scores it, and PPO updates the policy to make higher-scoring answers likelier.

steps.heading: Reward-model score versus actual human preference
steps.caption: The KL leash — without a penalty for drifting from the reference model, the policy finds text that games the reward model rather than pleasing people.

steps.heading: What has to be running
steps.caption: The operational cost — RLHF needs a reward model, a policy, a frozen reference, and a stable RL loop. That is a lot of moving parts.

dpo.title: DPO: preference tuning without the RL loop
dpo.description: Same preference data as RLHF, no reward model, no sampling loop — one supervised-style objective on the pairs directly.

steps.heading: A DPO training triple
steps.caption: Same input data — prompt, chosen response, rejected response. Nothing about the labelling changes from RLHF.

steps.heading: Log-probabilities before the update
steps.caption: No reward model — instead of scoring text with a second network, DPO reads the log-probabilities the policy already assigns to each response.

steps.heading: Implicit reward: β·(log π_θ − log π_ref)
steps.caption: The objective — raise the chosen response's probability relative to the reference, and lower the rejected one's, in a single loss.

steps.heading: Pipeline comparison
steps.caption: Side by side — DPO removes the reward model and the sampling loop. Two models in memory instead of three, and no PPO to stabilise.

steps.heading: Effect of annotator bias, either method
steps.caption: Shared limitation — both methods inherit whatever is in the preference data. Simpler machinery does not mean better judgement.

overfit-underfit.title: Underfitting and overfitting
overfit-underfit.description: Three training runs on the same data, told apart by the gap between the training curve and the validation curve.

steps.heading: Linear model on a curved relationship
steps.caption: Underfitting — both curves stay high and close together. The model is too small or trained too briefly to capture the pattern.

steps.heading: Right-sized model, diverse data
steps.caption: A good fit — both curves fall and stay close. The model learned the signal and stopped there.

steps.heading: Large model on a small, repetitive dataset
steps.caption: Overfitting — training error keeps falling while validation error turns upward. The model is memorising examples, not learning the rule.

steps.heading: Validation error after each intervention
steps.caption: Remedies — more and more diverse data, regularisation, or simply stopping earlier. All of them shrink the gap rather than the training error.

steps.heading: Memorisation in large models
steps.caption: For LLMs it becomes a privacy issue — an overfitted model can reproduce training text verbatim, including data that should never leave.
